title: "No blame on you today"
hook: a grieving father who never despairs, a brother who forgives, and a shirt that brings back sight
carry: forgive one old thing, out loud
tomorrow: the vow and the fruit out of season

segments.voice: Yesterday, cup: the brothers at the gate, with no idea who was filling their sacks. Your line was he knew them.

The brothers go home without the youngest, and the eldest stays in Egypt, unwilling to face his father. First Yusuf, now his little brother too. Ya'qub turns away, and the Qur'an says his eyes went white with grief. His sons think he'll grieve himself to death. He answers: “I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah.” Then he sends them back: look for Yusuf and his brother, and “despair not of the Spirit of Allah.” They return a third time, poor, begging for grain as charity. The powerful man across the table asks quietly: do you know what you did to Yusuf? They stare. Are you Yusuf?
screen: `A FATHER'S EYES GO WHITE.` → `DESPAIR NOT.` → `ARE YOU YUSUF?`

segments.voice: I am Yusuf, he says, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. They threw him in a well, sold him for a few coins, lied to their father with false blood. After years as a servant and a prisoner, he holds the grain of Egypt, and they stand before him with empty sacks. They admit it: Allah has preferred you over us, and we were wrong. Yusuf's answer is la tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm. No blame on you today. No reproach, no list of what you did. Then: may Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of those who show mercy. He doesn't make them earn it. He doesn't wait for them to grovel. Then the shirt returns, one last time. The first came home with false blood. The second, torn from behind, proved him innocent. Now Yusuf sends a third: lay this on my father's face. Before the caravan arrives, Ya'qub says, I can smell Yusuf. The shirt touches his face, and he sees again. The whole family comes to Egypt. Yusuf raises his parents up beside him, and they all bow down. Yusuf says: “This is the interpretation of my dream of old.” Eleven stars, sun and moon, from day one of this story. And when Yusuf tells the story back, he says Shaytan made trouble between me and my brothers. Even then, he won't name them as villains. Years later, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported to have answered his old enemies in Mecca with these same words.
screen: `I AM YUSUF, AND THIS IS MY BROTHER.` · `NO BLAME ON YOU TODAY.` · `THE THIRD SHIRT: HIS FATHER SEES.` · `THE DREAM COMES TRUE.` · then, large: `DESPAIR NOT OF THE SPIRIT OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Let one old hurt come up, not the biggest, one that still stings, a sibling's wrong word years ago, and picture their face. Forgive it out loud, to the room; you don't have to feel it all the way, and today is enough. If you pray, ask Allah to forgive them, the way Yusuf did.
Tathrib, reproach: the word Yusuf set aside when he told his brothers, no blame on you today.
Your line: forgive one old thing, out loud. Fourteen days of Yusuf, from a dream to a dream come true; tomorrow, Maryam. Day sixty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Muslims often recall Yusuf's words to his brothers when making peace after a quarrel, and many read Surah Yusuf in full as a story of patience, trust and forgiveness.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about letting it go.
what it means: Yusuf, holding all the power, refuses to scold the brothers who sold him, and asks Allah to forgive them.
what a scholar hears: tathrib is reproach, rebuking someone with their faults. tradition reports that the Prophet ﷺ echoed Yusuf's words when he forgave the people of Mecca.

notes: The index word is the full title in quotation marks ("No blame on you today"); kept exactly as the index has it.
Pickthall 12:86, 12:87 and 12:100 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording. 12:92 is paraphrased (Pickthall renders it roughly 'Have no fear this day!'; confirm and consider quoting).

Report that the Prophet quoted Yusuf's words ('I say to you what my brother Yusuf said') at the conquest of Mecca: found in seerah and in al-Bayhaqi's Sunan al-Kubra; strength of chain debated. Stated as 'is reported'. Confirm.

'Raises his parents up beside him' follows 12:100 ('raised his parents up on the throne'). Many commentators say 'parents' here includes his mother or his aunt/stepmother; the script says 'parents' without deciding. Confirm.
The prostration in 12:100 is understood by commentators as a bow of greeting/honor permitted in earlier law, not worship. The script says 'bow down'. Confirm whether a note is wanted.
